options.text: The model checks whether its output is statistically plausible, not whether it is true.
The model runs out of memory and invents filler text.
Users write prompts that are too short.
A bug in the training software that vendors are close to fixing.

questions.explanation: The model predicts what text is likely to come next rather than verifying facts, so a pattern that looks right — such as a plausible-sounding citation — will be produced regardless of whether it matches reality.

questions.text: Hallucinations are a temporary bug that will be eliminated in the next generation of models.
questions.explanation: The lesson calls hallucinations a fundamental consequence of how language models work: as long as text is generated by statistical prediction rather than factual verification, they remain possible.

questions.text: Which tasks does the lesson list as genuine strengths of AI?

options.text: Generating first drafts of lesson plans, worksheets or emails
Brainstorming and generating many ideas quickly
Explaining a concept in different ways and at different levels

questions.explanation: First drafts, brainstorming, alternative explanations, reformatting and translation are named as strengths, while specific citations and multi-step calculations are listed among the things AI consistently struggles with.

questions.text: What practical advice does the lesson give for complex, multi-step tasks?

options.text: Provide all critical information in a single, well-organised message.
Spread the information over as many short messages as possible.
Ask the same question several times and average the answers.
Ask the model to memorise the task permanently.

questions.explanation: Because the context window is limited, critical information should be given upfront rather than relying on the model to remember details from many messages ago.
